lessons.title: Beam and Column Fabrication
lessons.body: Beams and columns are the backbone of any steel structure. In Africa, we often use universal beams (UB) and universal columns (UC) imported or locally rolled. Your job is to cut, drill, and weld them to exact lengths and shapes. Start by studying the fabrication drawings. Mark cut lengths with a chalk line or soapstone, allowing for shrinkageâabout 1.5 mm per metre for welding. Use a band saw or oxy-fuel torch to cut. For clean cuts, a plasma cutter works well on thinner sections. After cutting, grind the ends square. For columns, you may need to weld base plates and cap plates. Base plates are usually 20â25 mm thick, with holes for anchor bolts. Position the plate, check squareness with a try square, and tack weld. Then weld all around with a 3 mm root gap. Use E7018 electrodes for strength. For beams, you might need to cope the ends to fit into connections. A beam-to-column connection often requires notching the beam flanges. Use a template to mark the cope, then cut with a torch and grind smooth. Always preheat thick sections (over 25 mm) to 100â150Â°C before welding to prevent cracking. In many African workshops, you'll use a 350A inverter welder. Set it to 130â150A for 3.2 mm electrodes. After welding, clean slag and inspect for undercut or porosity. Finally, mark the member with its piece mark using a paint pen or metal stamp. This ensures correct assembly on site. Remember, a beam cut 5 mm short is scrap. Measure twice, cut once.

lessons.title: Truss and Girder Fabrication
lessons.body: Trusses and girders carry heavy loads over long spans. In Africa, they are common in warehouses, churches, and bridges. A truss is made of chords (top and bottom) and web members (diagonals and verticals). Girders are deep beams, often welded from plates. Start with a jigâa flat steel table or concrete slab where you can assemble the truss. Mark the node points using a tape measure and chalk. Cut all members to length, allowing for gusset plates. Gusset plates are typically 8â12 mm thick. For a 12 m span truss, use angles like 75x75x6 mm for chords and 50x50x5 mm for webs. Assemble the truss on the jig, clamp members, and check diagonals with a tape measureâthey must be equal. Tack weld all joints. Then weld fully using a sequence to avoid distortion: weld opposite sides alternately. Use E6013 electrodes for general work, or E7018 for high strength. For girders, you may need to weld web to flanges with a continuous fillet weld. Use a 4 mm electrode at 160â180A. To prevent twisting, weld in a back-step pattern. After welding, check straightness with a string line. If the truss is warped, apply heat with a torch and correct with a hydraulic jack. Finally, drill holes for connectionsâusually 18 mm for M16 bolts. Paint with red oxide primer. In rural areas, you might use a generator-powered welder. Always wear a welding helmet and gloves. A well-made truss can last 50 years if protected from rust.

lessons.title: Connection Design and Detailing
lessons.body: Connections transfer forces between members. They are designed by engineers but fabricated by you. Common connections: bolted, welded, and riveted (rare today). For bolted connections, you need to drill holes accurately. Use a magnetic drill or a pillar drill. Hole diameter is usually 2 mm larger than bolt diameter. For M20 bolts, drill 22 mm holes. Mark hole positions from the drawing using a template. Clamp members together and drill through both at onceâthis ensures alignment. Deburr holes with a grinder. For welded connections, prepare the edges: bevel 30Â° for full penetration welds. Use a 3 mm root gap and tack weld. Then weld in multiple passes. For a moment connection (beam to column), you might weld the beam flanges directly to the column and bolt the web. This requires a backing plate. In Africa, we often use simple shear connections: a fin plate welded to the column and bolted to the beam web. Fin plates are 10 mm thick, with 3â4 bolts. Always check bolt torque: for M20 grade 8.8, torque to 400 Nm. Use a torque wrench. If not available, use the turn-of-nut method: snug tight, then turn 1/3 turn. For welded connections, inspect with a magnifying glass for cracks. Remember, a connection that fails can collapse the whole structure. So, follow the drawing exactly. If something doesn't fit, don't force itâreport to the engineer.

lessons.title: Steel Decking and Joists
lessons.body: Steel decking and joists form floors and roofs. In Africa, they are used in multi-storey buildings and industrial sheds. Steel decking is a corrugated sheet, usually 0.9â1.2 mm thick, galvanised. It sits on beams and is filled with concrete. Joists are open-web steel bars (like a mini truss) or rolled sections. For decking, start by cutting sheets to length with a nibbler or angle grinder. Overlap sheets by one corrugation and fasten with self-drilling screws (12â14 x 20 mm) every 300 mm. At the ends, use shear studsâwelded through the deck to the beam. Use a stud welding gun. Studs are typically 19 mm diameter, 100 mm long. After welding, bend the stud 30Â° to testâif it doesn't break, it's good. For joists, they are often prefabricated. You just need to cut and weld end plates. A common joist is the SJI (Steel Joist Institute) type. For a 6 m span, you might use a 200 mm deep joist. Place joists at 1.2 m centres. Weld or bolt them to the supporting beams. Use a spacer to keep them parallel. After installation, decking is laid and concrete poured. In hot African climates, ensure decking is not walked on before concreteâit can buckle. Use temporary props every 2 m. Finally, check that all screws are tight and studs are welded. A good decking job saves concrete and speeds construction.

lessons.title: Erection and Field Assembly
lessons.body: Erection is where the structure goes up. In Africa, this is often done with a mobile crane or a chain hoist. Before erection, ensure all members are marked and delivered to site in order. Check the foundation boltsâthey must be within 3 mm of the drawing. Use a template to set them. Start by erecting the first bay: two columns and a beam. Use a crane to lift columns, then bolt to base plates. Plumb the column with a spirit level and adjust with shims. Tighten anchor bolts to 200 Nm. Then lift the beam and connect. Use drift pins to align holes. Once the first bay is stable, add temporary guying (cables) to keep it plumb. Continue with adjacent bays. For trusses, assemble on the ground first, then lift as a unit. Use a spreader bar to prevent damage. Bolting: use impact wrenches for speed, but final torque with a torque wrench. For welded connections on site, use E7018 electrodes and preheat if cold. In remote areas, you might use a generator and a 300A welder. Safety: never stand under a suspended load. Use tag lines to control members. After erection, check alignment with a total station or plumb bob. Tighten all bolts after final alignment. Finally, apply touch-up paint to welds and scratches. A well-erected structure can be completed 30% faster than one with poor planning.

lessons.title: Case Studies of Structural Projects
lessons.body: Let's look at real African projects. Case 1: A warehouse in Nairobi, Kenya. Span 24 m, trusses at 6 m centres. Fabricated with locally available 100x100x10 angles. Welded with E6013. Erection took 3 weeks with a 20-ton crane. Total steel weight: 45 tonnes. Cost: $2,500 per tonne. Case 2: A pedestrian bridge in Kampala, Uganda. Main girders: welded plate girders, 12 m long, 800 mm deep. Flanges 300x20 mm, web 800x10 mm. Welded with E7018, preheated to 120Â°C. Bolted connections on site. Challenge: transport to site was difficult, so they assembled in two halves and bolted mid-span. Case 3: A multi-storey office in Lagos, Nigeria. Used steel decking on beams. Decking 1.2 mm thick, studs 19 mm. Concrete 150 mm thick. Saved 20% on concrete compared to traditional slab. Case 4: A church in Accra, Ghana. Trusses 18 m span, made from recycled steel pipes. Welded with a generator welder. Despite limited resources, the structure stood strong. Lessons: Always use jigs for repetitive work. Pre-drill holes to avoid site problems. Protect steel from rust with primer and paint. In Africa, logistics and power supply are big challengesâplan for backup generators. Also, train your team on safety. Many accidents happen from falls or falling loads. Use harnesses and hard hats. Finally, document everything: photos, measurements, and material certificates. This helps in future projects and for client approval.

quiz.q: What is the typical allowance for welding shrinkage per metre?
quiz.explanation: A common rule is 1.5 mm per metre to compensate for weld shrinkage.

quiz.q: Which electrode is preferred for high-strength structural welds?
quiz.explanation: E7018 is a low-hydrogen electrode giving high strength and crack resistance.

quiz.q: For a 12 m span truss, what size angles are commonly used for chords?
quiz.explanation: 75x75x6 mm angles are typical for chords in a 12 m span truss.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a jig in truss fabrication?
options: B) To hold members in place during assembly
quiz.explanation: A jig holds members accurately while tack welding.

quiz.q: How much larger should a bolt hole be than the bolt diameter?
quiz.explanation: Standard practice is 2 mm larger for ease of assembly.

quiz.q: What is the torque for an M20 grade 8.8 bolt?
quiz.explanation: 400 Nm is the typical torque for M20 grade 8.8 bolts.

quiz.q: Which connection type is most common in African steel workshops?
quiz.explanation: Bolted connections are preferred for ease and speed on site.

quiz.q: What is the minimum preheat for welding 25 mm thick steel?
quiz.explanation: 100â150Â°C preheat prevents cracking in thick sections.

quiz.q: What is the typical thickness of steel decking?
quiz.explanation: Decking is usually 0.9 to 1.2 mm thick galvanised sheet.

quiz.q: How are shear studs tested?
quiz.explanation: Bending a stud 30Â° tests weld integrity.

quiz.q: What is the maximum spacing of self-drilling screws in decking?
quiz.explanation: Screws are typically spaced at 300 mm along seams.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of temporary guying during erection?
quiz.explanation: Guy cables prevent the structure from twisting or falling.

quiz.q: What tool is used to align bolt holes during erection?
quiz.explanation: Drift pins align holes without damaging threads.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost per tonne of fabricated steel in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Case study showed $2,500 per tonne for a warehouse.

quiz.q: What was the main challenge in the Kampala pedestrian bridge?
quiz.explanation: Transport to site was difficult, so they assembled in halves.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of steel decking over traditional slab?
quiz.explanation: Decking acts as formwork and saves concrete volume.

quiz.q: What is the first step in beam fabrication?
quiz.explanation: Cutting to length is the first step after marking.

quiz.q: What is the root gap for a full penetration weld?
quiz.explanation: A 3 mm root gap ensures full penetration.

quiz.q: What is the typical bolt diameter for a fin plate connection?
quiz.explanation: M20 bolts are common for fin plate shear connections.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a backing plate in a moment connection?
options: B) To ensure full penetration weld
quiz.explanation: Backing plates help achieve full penetration welds.

quiz.q: What is the maximum span for a 200 mm deep open-web joist?
quiz.explanation: A 200 mm joist typically spans up to 6 m.

quiz.q: What is the typical spacing of joists in a floor system?
quiz.explanation: Joists are commonly spaced at 1.2 m centres.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to check before erection?
quiz.explanation: Foundation bolts must be within tolerance for columns to fit.

quiz.q: What is the maximum tolerance for foundation bolt position?
quiz.explanation: Typically within 3 mm of drawing position.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a spreader bar during lifting?
options: B) To prevent damage to truss
quiz.explanation: Spreader bars distribute load and prevent sling damage.

quiz.q: What is the final step after erection?
quiz.explanation: Touch-up paint protects welds and scratches from rust.

quiz.q: In the Lagos office case study, what was saved by using decking?
quiz.explanation: Decking saved 20% on concrete compared to traditional slab.

quiz.q: What material was used for the Accra church trusses?
quiz.explanation: The case study mentioned recycled steel pipes.

quiz.q: What is a key safety rule during erection?
quiz.explanation: Tag lines control loads and keep workers safe.

quiz.q: What is the typical welding current for a 4 mm electrode?
quiz.explanation: 4 mm electrodes run at about 160â180 A.
